note.explanation: Mitosis makes two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. It has two major parts: karyokinesis, the division of the nucleus, and cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.
examples: When skin cells are replaced, mitosis makes new cells that are exact copies of older cells.
In Hydra, mitosis helps a bud grow into a new individual.
note.simple: Mitosis is like copying a cell: the copied chromosomes are shared between two new cells, so each new cell has the same chromosome number as the original.
note.checkQuestion: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate?
note.title: Mitosis: making two matching cells
steps: First, the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
The result is two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
note.answer: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell.

mcqs.stem: During which phase do chromosomes attached to spindle fibres arrange along the cell equator?
rationales: Prophase is when chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
Metaphase is correct because chromosomes arrange along the equator to form the metaphase plate.
Anaphase is when sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles.
Telophase is when new nuclear envelopes form around the separated chromosome sets.

mcqs.stem: Which event occurs during anaphase of mitosis?
rationales: The nuclear envelope breaks down during prophase.
Sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles during anaphase.
The nucleolus reforms during telophase.
A cleavage furrow moves inward during cytokinesis in animal cells.

mcqs.stem: What is the division of the cytoplasm called?
rationales: Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus.
Cytokinesis is correct because it is the division of the cytoplasm.
Metaphase is a phase of karyokinesis, not the division of cytoplasm.
Regeneration is the formation of new body parts, not a cell-division phase.

options: The cell forms a cleavage furrow.
The cell makes a phragmoplast from Golgi vesicles.
Chromosomes line up at the equator.
mcqs.stem: Which event is associated with cytokinesis in plant cells?
rationales: A cleavage furrow forms in animal cells during cytokinesis.
In plant cells, Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to form a plate called a phragmoplast.
Plant cells do not have centrosomes; their mitotic spindle forms from spindle fibres in the cytoplasm.
Chromosomes line up at the equator during metaphase, not during plant-cell cytokinesis.

options: Chromosomes line up along the equator.
mcqs.stem: Which event takes place during telophase?
rationales: During telophase, both sets of chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Centrosomes duplicate and migrate during prophase.
Chromosomes line up along the equator during metaphase.
Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

options: The daughter cells have half the parent cell's chromosome number.
The daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
Only one daughter cell is formed.
The daughter cells receive no chromosomes.
mcqs.stem: What is the chromosome-number outcome of mitosis?
rationales: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number; that is associated with meiosis.
Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
Mitosis produces two daughter cells, not one.
The chromosomes are distributed between the daughter cells; they do not both receive none.

options: A cell receives both sister chromosomes while the other receives none.
The chromosomes line up at the equator.
The cell forms a cleavage furrow.
mcqs.stem: What can happen if sister chromatids fail to separate during anaphase?
rationales: If sister chromatids fail to separate, one daughter cell may receive both sister chromosomes and the other none.
Chromosome alignment at the equator is a normal event of metaphase.
Nucleolus reformation is a normal event of telophase.
A cleavage furrow is a normal feature of cytokinesis in animal cells.

mcqs.stem: What is a tumour called if it migrates and invades other tissues?
rationales: A benign tumour remains in its original location.
A malignant tumour is correct because it can migrate and invade other tissues.
A metaphase plate is the arrangement of chromosomes at the cell equator.
A phragmoplast is a plate formed during cytokinesis in plant cells.

written.text: During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?

rubric.why: The phase name identifies when separation occurs.
rubric.how: State that it is anaphase.

rubric.why: The question asks specifically about the event involving sister chromatids.
rubric.how: Explain that sister chromatids separate.

modelAnswer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

written.text: What is the role of spindle fibres in mitosis?
written.finalAnswer: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes at the centromere and pull the sister chromatids towards opposite poles during anaphase.

rubric.why: The attachment point explains how spindle fibres connect to chromosomes.
rubric.how: State that spindle fibres attach to chromosomes at the centromere.

rubric.why: Their pulling action moves chromatids to opposite ends of the cell.
rubric.how: State that the fibres pull sister chromatids towards opposite poles.

modelAnswer: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes at the centromere.
During anaphase, they pull the sister chromatids towards opposite poles.

written.text: How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?
written.finalAnswer: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator and moves inward, pinching the cell into two. In plant cells, Golgi vesicles move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast; the plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane.

rubric.why: The inward-moving furrow is the key feature of animal-cell cytokinesis.
rubric.how: Mention the furrow moving inward and pinching the cell.

rubric.why: The vesicles and plate formation describe the plant-cell method.
rubric.how: Mention Golgi vesicles forming a phragmoplast that grows outward.

modelAnswer: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator.
The ring contracts and the furrow moves inward, pinching the parent cell into two.
In plant cells, Golgi apparatus makes vesicles that move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast.
The plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane, resulting in two daughter cells.

written.text: What are the key events of anaphase in mitosis?
written.finalAnswer: Spindle fibres attached with chromosomes pull toward the poles. The sister chromatids separate, forming two similar sets of chromatids that move towards the poles of the cell.

rubric.why: The spindle fibres' pulling action causes the chromosome sets to move.
rubric.how: State that spindle fibres pull towards the poles.

rubric.why: Separation of sister chromatids is the defining event of anaphase.
rubric.how: State that sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles.

modelAnswer: The spindle fibres attached with chromosomes pull toward the poles.
The chromosome's sister chromatids separate.
Two similar sets of chromatids move towards the poles of the cell.

written.text: What is the function of the centrosome during cell division?
written.finalAnswer: The centrosome duplicates and the two centrosomes migrate to opposite sides of the nucleus. They make a network of microtubules called spindle fibres, which form the mitotic spindle.

rubric.why: The centrosomes duplicate and move to opposite sides to organise division.
rubric.how: Mention duplication and migration to opposite sides of the nucleus.

rubric.why: Spindle formation is the centrosome's central contribution to mitosis.
rubric.how: Name the spindle fibres or mitotic spindle.

modelAnswer: The centrosome duplicates into two centrosomes.
The two centrosomes migrate to opposite sides of the nucleus.
They make spindle fibres, whose complete set is called the mitotic spindle.

written.text: How is mitosis related to the process of regeneration?
written.finalAnswer: Some animals regenerate parts of the body. For this purpose, they form new cells by carrying out mitosis in the cells of the remaining parts.

rubric.why: Regeneration needs new cells to replace or rebuild the missing body part.
rubric.how: Explain that mitosis forms new cells.

rubric.why: This links mitosis to the rebuilding of a body part.
rubric.how: State that animals use mitosis in remaining cells to regenerate body parts.

modelAnswer: Some animals can regenerate parts of the body.
For this purpose, they form new cells by carrying out mitosis in the cells of the remaining parts.

written.text: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
written.finalAnswer: Karyokinesis consists of prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. In prophase, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, the nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and spindle fibres form. In metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres and arrange along the equator. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles. In telophase, new nuclear envelopes form, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold into chromatin. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm to form two daughter cells.

rubric.why: Prophase begins chromosome condensation and formation of the mitotic spindle.
rubric.how: Mention condensed chromosomes and the breakdown of the nuclear envelope or formation of spindle fibres.

rubric.why: Chromosome alignment at the equator identifies metaphase.
rubric.how: State that chromosomes attach to spindle fibres and line up at the equator.

rubric.why: Chromatid separation and movement to opposite poles identify anaphase.
rubric.how: State that sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles.

rubric.why: Nuclear reformation and chromosome unfolding identify telophase.
rubric.how: Mention new nuclear envelopes and chromosomes unfolding into chromatin.

rubric.why: The final answer must explain how division produces two cells.
rubric.how: State that cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to form two daughter cells.

modelAnswer: Karyokinesis means division of the nucleus and is divided into four phases.
During prophase, thread-like chromatin condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.
The nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down, and spindle fibres form.
During metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres at the centromere and arrange along the equator, forming the metaphase plate.
During anaphase, spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids apart towards opposite poles.
During telophase, a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and results in two daughter cells.

written.text: Describe cytokinesis in animal and plant cells.
written.finalAnswer: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator. A ring of microfilaments contracts, causing the furrow to move inward and pinch the parent cell into two. In plant cells, Golgi apparatus makes vesicles that move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast. The plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane, resulting in two daughter cells.

rubric.why: The furrow at the equator is the starting point of animal-cell cytokinesis.
rubric.how: State that a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator.

rubric.why: Contraction and inward movement explain how an animal cell divides.
rubric.how: Mention the contracting ring and inward-moving furrow.

rubric.why: Vesicles forming a phragmoplast are the plant-cell method.
rubric.description: Describe formation of the plant-cell plate.
rubric.how: State that Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to form a phragmoplast.

rubric.why: Growth of the plate and its fusion with the membrane complete division.
rubric.how: State that the plate grows outward and results in two daughter cells.

modelAnswer: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator.
At this furrow, the cytoplasm has a ring of microfilaments.
The ring contracts and the furrow moves inward, pinching the parent cell into two.
In plant cells, Golgi apparatus makes vesicles that move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast.
The plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane.
The result is two daughter cells.

written.finalAnswer: Mitosis is significant in growth, cell replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction. It increases the number of cells for growth, replaces dying cells with exact copies, forms new cells for regeneration, and enables organisms such as Hydra to reproduce asexually by budding.

rubric.why: Mitosis increases cell number and so contributes to growth.
rubric.how: Link mitosis to an increase in the number of cells.

rubric.why: Mitosis replaces cells that constantly die in the body.
rubric.how: State that new cells replace dying cells.

rubric.why: New cells formed by mitosis help some animals regenerate body parts.
rubric.how: Connect mitosis to forming cells in remaining body parts.

rubric.why: Mitosis supports asexual reproduction, such as budding in Hydra.
rubric.how: Give Hydra budding as an example.

rubric.why: The final answer should note that mitosis produces matching cells.
rubric.description: State the importance of the daughter cells.
rubric.how: Mention that the new cells are identical or exact copies.

modelAnswer: Growth occurs due to an increase in the number of cells.
Mitosis produces new cells that are identical to the original cells and plays a crucial role in growth.
Many cells constantly die in the body; mitosis forms new cells that are exact copies of the older cells to replace them.
Some animals regenerate parts of the body by forming new cells through mitosis in the cells of the remaining parts.
Mitosis is a means for asexual reproduction; for example, in Hydra it forms a bud that grows into a new individual.

written.text: What role might mistakes in the cell cycle checkpoints play in the emergence of cancer?
written.finalAnswer: If cell-cycle checkpoints fail to stop cells with errors from dividing, cells may divide uncontrollably. Masses of cells called tumours can form; if they invade other tissues, they are malignant tumours (cancer), and their spread is called metastasis.

rubric.why: The answer must connect checkpoint failure with cells not being stopped when they have errors.
rubric.how: State that checkpoints may fail to stop cells with errors from dividing.

rubric.why: Uncontrolled cell division is the key consequence of failed regulation.
rubric.how: Explain that the cells continue dividing uncontrollably.

rubric.why: The mass formed by uncontrolled division is called a tumour.
rubric.how: State that masses of cells called tumours can form.

rubric.why: Invasion of other tissues identifies malignant tumours, or cancer.
rubric.how: Mention malignant tumours and invasion or spread to other tissues.

modelAnswer: If cell-cycle checkpoints fail to stop cells with errors from dividing, the cells may continue dividing uncontrollably.
Masses of cells formed by uncontrolled division are called tumours.
If tumours migrate and invade other tissues, they are called malignant tumours (cancer).
The spread of disease is called metastasis.

steps.why: Naming the two major parts gives the structure for describing the complete process.
steps.text: There are two major phases of mitosis i.e. karyokinesis and cytokinesis.

steps.why: Prophase starts the nuclear division by making chromosomes visible and forming spindle fibres.
steps.text: During prophase, the thread-like chromatin material condenses and makes thick visible chromosomes.

steps.why: Metaphase is identified by chromosome alignment along the cell equator.
steps.text: The chromosomes attached with spindle fibres arrange themselves along the equator of the cell.

steps.why: The separation and movement of sister chromatids are the main events of anaphase.
steps.text: The chromosome's sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles of the cell.

steps.why: Telophase rebuilds the nuclei around the separated chromosome sets.
steps.text: In this phase, new nuclear envelope forms around each set of separated chromosomes and nucleolus reforms.

steps.why: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm after the nucleus has divided.
steps.text: Cytokinesis is the division of cytoplasm.

example.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
example.answer: Karyokinesis occurs through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm to form two daughter cells.

explain.title: What mitosis does
explain.body: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell. It occurs in the somatic cells of eukaryotes.

explain.title: The two major parts
explain.body: There are two major phases of mitosis i.e. karyokinesis and cytokinesis. Karyokinesis means the division of the nucleus. Cytokinesis is the division of cytoplasm.

explain.title: The four phases of karyokinesis
explain.body: In prophase, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down. In metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres and line up at the equator. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles. In telophase, new nuclear envelopes form, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.

explain.title: Cytokinesis in animal and plant cells
explain.body: In animal cells, a furrow develops at the equator and a ring of microfilaments contracts, pinching the cell into two. In plant cells, Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to form a plate called phragmoplast; it grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane.

explain.title: Why mitosis matters and what can go wrong
explain.body: Mitosis supports growth, cell replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction. If mitosis is not properly regulated, cells may divide uncontrollably and form tumours. Tumours that invade other tissues are malignant tumours (cancer); spreading of disease is called metastasis.

mistakes: Do not say mitosis halves the chromosome number: each daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
Do not mix up anaphase and metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase, while sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
Do not confuse karyokinesis with cytokinesis: karyokinesis is division of the nucleus, while cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm.
Do not describe plant cytokinesis as an inward-moving cleavage furrow; the book describes Golgi vesicles forming a plate that grows outward.
Do not call every tumour cancer: a tumour that stays in its original location is benign; a tumour that invades other tissues is malignant.
